title: Production Patterns
description: Typed HTTP clients, retry/backoff, structured logging, health checks, and infra-as-code shapes — real production patterns.

challenges.title: Typed HTTP client interface
challenges.whyMatters: A typed HTTP client interface means every API call site knows what it receives — no runtime guessing about response shapes.
hints: Generics let the return type flow from the call site to the type system

choices.label: A)  returns any — no type safety
B)  generic methods with typed responses
C)  typeof fetch is too broad and not typed per-endpoint
D)  describes a request, not a client

challenges.title: Retry with exponential backoff — concept
challenges.description:
In a retry with exponential backoff, if the base delay is 100ms and the multiplier is 2, what are the delays before attempts 1, 2, 3, 4?

  (attempt 0 = first try, no delay).
challenges.whyMatters: Exponential backoff prevents thundering herd — when 100 services all retry at the same fixed interval, they overwhelm the recovering dependency together.
hints: delay = base * multiplier^attempt — so attempt 1 = 100*2^1

choices.label: 100ms, 100ms, 100ms (fixed delay)
100ms, 200ms, 300ms (linear)

challenges.title: Write a retry with backoff
challenges.description:
Write a generic function:

  retry<T>(fn: () => Promise<T>, options: RetryOptions): Promise<T>

Where:
  interface RetryOptions { maxAttempts: number; baseDelayMs: number; multiplier: number }

Behavior:
- Call fn()
- On success: return the value
- On failure: wait baseDelayMs * multiplier^attempt ms, then retry
- After maxAttempts total tries, throw the last error
- Each attempt number starts at 0

Also export a `delay(ms: number): Promise<void>` helper.
challenges.whyMatters: This is the single most common resilience pattern in production tooling. You will write or use this in every service that makes external calls.
hints: Use a for loop from 0 to maxAttempts - 1
Wrap fn() in try/catch — save the error, delay, continue
After the loop, throw the last saved error
delay = baseDelayMs * Math.pow(multiplier, attempt)

challenges.title: Structured logging types
challenges.whyMatters: Structured logs (JSON lines) are machine-parseable — they flow into Datadog, Grafana Loki, and CloudWatch without regex parsing. Typed log calls prevent missing required fields.
hints: The type enforces the shape at every call site — you can't forget timestamp or use an invalid level

choices.label: No advantage — console.log is equally typed
Every log call is type-checked — missing fields or invalid levels are compile errors, and output is parseable JSON
It is faster than console.log at runtime
It prevents log injection attacks

challenges.title: Write a structured logger
challenges.description:
Build a structured logger:

  type LogLevel = 'debug' | 'info' | 'warn' | 'error'

  interface LogEntry { level: LogLevel; message: string; timestamp: string; service: string; fields?: Record<string, unknown> }

  interface Logger {
    debug(message: string, fields?: Record<string, unknown>): void
    info(message: string, fields?: Record<string, unknown>): void
    warn(message: string, fields?: Record<string, unknown>): void
    error(message: string, fields?: Record<string, unknown>): void
  }

Write `createLogger(service: string): Logger` — each method outputs a JSON line to stdout with the current ISO timestamp.

Also write `withFields(logger: Logger, fields: Record<string, unknown>): Logger` — returns a new logger that merges the given fields into every log call.
challenges.whyMatters: Every software engineering tool you build needs structured logging. createLogger + withFields is the factory pattern used in real logging libraries like pino.
hints: Implement a private log(level, message, fields) method, call it from each public method
new Date().toISOString() for timestamp
withFields wraps each method: (msg, f) => logger.info(msg, { ...fields, ...f })
Use process.stdout.write(JSON.stringify(entry) + '\n') for clean output

challenges.title: Health check result types
challenges.description:
Which design is better for a health check system that needs to report per-dependency status?

  A)  function healthCheck(): boolean
  B)  function healthCheck(): Promise<{ db: boolean; cache: boolean; queue: boolean }>
  C)  function healthCheck(): Promise<Record<string, { ok: boolean; latencyMs: number; error?: string }>>
  D)  function healthCheck(): Promise<string>
challenges.whyMatters: Health checks that return rich structured data can drive dashboards, alerting, and dependency graphs. A boolean tells you nothing about which dependency failed or how slow it was.
hints: Think about what a downstream dashboard or alert rule needs to consume

choices.label: A)  boolean — too little information
B)  hardcoded dependency names — breaks when you add a new dependency
C)  Record with rich per-dependency data — extensible and informative
D)  string — unstructured, untyped

challenges.title: Write a health check aggregator
challenges.description:
Write a health check system:

  interface HealthResult { ok: boolean; latencyMs: number; error?: string }
  type HealthReport = Record<string, HealthResult>
  type HealthCheck = () => Promise<HealthResult>

Write `runHealthChecks(checks: Record<string, HealthCheck>): Promise<HealthReport>` that:
- Runs all checks in parallel
- Records latency for each (use Date.now() before/after)
- If a check throws, records ok: false with the error message
- Never rejects — always returns a full report

Write `isHealthy(report: HealthReport): boolean` — true only if ALL checks passed.

Write `summarize(report: HealthReport): string` — returns `"3/4 healthy: db(12ms) cache(5ms) queue(FAILED: connection refused) api(8ms)"`
challenges.whyMatters: This is a production health check endpoint. The pattern — parallel checks, latency tracking, never-throw, summary — is used verbatim in real services.
hints: Map checks entries to promises, use Promise.all (each check wrapped in try/catch)
Record latency: const start = Date.now(); try { result = await check() } finally { latency = Date.now() - start }
summarize: count ok, then map each entry to name(Xms) or name(FAILED: error)

challenges.title: Infra-as-code type shapes
challenges.description:
Why is this Pulumi-style pattern valuable?

  interface Resource<T extends string, P extends object> {
    type: T
    name: string
    properties: P
  }

  type BucketResource = Resource<'aws:s3:Bucket', { bucketName: string; versioning: boolean }>
  type FunctionResource = Resource<'aws:lambda:Function', { handler: string; runtime: string; memoryMb: number }>
challenges.whyMatters: Typed resource definitions catch property typos and missing fields at compile time — before a terraform apply or pulumi up that would fail after a 3-minute plan.
hints: Think about what errors you catch at compile time vs. runtime

choices.label: The generic makes the type flexible enough to accept any resource without type errors
Each resource type has a distinct property shape — wrong properties on BucketResource are compile errors, not runtime surprises
It is just documentation — no actual type safety is added
It prevents runtime errors in AWS

challenges.title: Build a typed deployment pipeline
challenges.description:
Build a minimal typed deployment pipeline:

  type Stage = 'build' | 'test' | 'deploy' | 'verify'
  type StageStatus = 'pending' | 'running' | 'passed' | 'failed'

  interface StageResult { stage: Stage; status: StageStatus; durationMs: number; output: string }
  interface PipelineResult { stages: StageResult[]; success: boolean; totalMs: number }

  type StageRunner = (stage: Stage) => Promise<{ output: string }>

Write `runPipeline(stages: Stage[], runner: StageRunner): Promise<PipelineResult>` that:
- Runs stages sequentially (not in parallel)
- Tracks status and duration for each stage
- Stops on first failure — remaining stages stay 'pending'
- Returns the full PipelineResult

Write `formatPipeline(result: PipelineResult): string` that produces:
  `"Pipeline: passed/failed (Xms)\n  ✓ build (120ms)\n  ✓ test (340ms)\n  ✗ deploy (50ms)\n  - verify (pending)"`
challenges.whyMatters: This pattern is the core of every CI/CD pipeline runner, deployment script, and runbook automator. Sequential stages, failure propagation, and structured results are universal.
hints: Use a for loop — await runner(stage) inside try/catch
On failure, push the failed result then break — push remaining stages as pending
Track totalMs with Date.now() at start and end of the whole pipeline
formatPipeline: map each result to icon + name + (Xms) or (pending)
